tip.title: Polite directions
tip.body: Start with perdone or disculpe ("excuse me"), then ¿dónde está …? People will answer with polite commands: siga (keep going), gire (turn), cruce (cross). Todo recto is "straight on" in Spain; in much of Latin America you'll hear derecho or todo derecho instead. Careful: a la derecha means "to the right", but derecho means "straight ahead".

tip.title: Little location words
tip.body: al lado de (next to), enfrente de (opposite), detrás de (behind), entre … y … (between … and …), al final de (at the end of). De + el becomes del: al lado del banco. Al final de la calle stays as it is.

lessons.title: hay or está?
lessons.goal: Say what there is and where things are.

tip.title: hay = there is, está = it is (located)
tip.body: Use hay ("there is / there are") to say that something exists, usually with un, una, numbers or no article: Hay un museo. Hay dos farmacias. Hay agua. It never changes. Use está (singular) or están (plural) to say where a specific, known thing is, with el, la, los, las or a name: El museo está en el centro. Las farmacias están en la plaza. So: ¿Hay un banco por aquí? (is there one at all?) but ¿Dónde está el banco? (where is the bank I know about?).

culture.title: Take the bus, don't "coger" it
culture.body: In Spain people say coger el autobús ("catch the bus"), but in Mexico, Argentina and other parts of Latin America coger is a vulgar word for having sex. Say tomar el autobús instead: it's correct everywhere. The bus itself has many names: autobús in Spain (understood everywhere), camión in Mexico, colectivo in Argentina and guagua in the Canary Islands and the Caribbean (Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic). Directions vary too: todo recto in Spain, derecho or todo derecho in much of Latin America.
